title: After a year building strategies with AI, here is what I learnt about building a backtesting engine for LLMs (to avoid overfitting)
author: LeastTangelo6022
selftext:
A few months ago I posted here about a year of vibe trading with AI. Short version: almost nothing survived honest validation. This is what I did next.



I gave AI agents a sealed holdout and let them hunt for trading strategies.



Each agent got one asset (10 assets, BTC to SUI) and data up to the end of 2024 only. At most 20 backtests each, every variant counted, one final strategy frozen. I wrote the pass criteria before any agent ran. Then I opened 2025–2026 once, with no retuning allowed.



\> 20 frozen finalists. 14 passed every in-sample check, with returns up to +2,900%.

\> Out-of-sample: \*\*0 out of 20 passed.\*\* The best one made +14.6% and still failed on win rate. Several lost more than half their money.



The agents weren't dumb. They were thorough, and thoroughness is exactly what turns noise into a beautiful equity curve.



AI doesn't overfit more than you. It overfits faster. A human tests 5 ideas and gets tired. An agent tests 500 and never does. Run enough variants and one will look amazing by luck. **If the backtester can't tell luck from edge, the AI will find the luck every time.**



So I stopped hunting strategies and rebuilt the backtester around that instead. Here is what a backtester built for AI agents needs.



**1. Data stamped with when you could have known it**

Most backtests use the time something happened. The time that matters is when it was available to you. Funding is written minutes after the hour. CPI comes out weeks after the month it describes, and gets revised. An options vendor publishes hours after midnight. Get one of these wrong and your AI trades on the future, and AI agents are very good at finding a one-bar lookahead. Every data point needs a "knowable at" stamp, and anything unclassified defaults to late.



**2. The same code in backtest and live**

If the live bot computes signals in a different codebase, you test one strategy and run another. Live should call the same functions on the same data, and say "not ready" when an input is missing instead of inventing a value.



**3. Real costs, on by default**

Fees, slippage and funding on every fill, with the after-cost number first. On a 52-strategy portfolio I ran, costs ate a fifth of the backtest return. An AI optimising gross numbers simply learns to trade more.



**4. Count every try**

Every variant the AI runs is a lottery ticket. The backtester should count them and say it plainly: "37 tries. Luck alone could reach a Sharpe of 1.2." If your strategy's Sharpe is 1.3, that's not an edge.



**5. A final exam the AI can't peek at**

Show in-sample and out-of-sample side by side on every run, but know its limit: after 50 variants, the out-of-sample part is in-sample too. The real test is data nobody touched. When a strategy is created, lock its last months. Every run, human or AI, stops before them. Open them once at the end, and stamp the result on the strategy forever, pass or fail.



**6. A stress test before you trust anything**

Reshuffle the trades to see the real worst drawdown. Double the costs. Nudge every setting by 15%. Replace the entries with random ones and check the signal beats a coin. Try it on similar assets. A real edge survives most of that. A lucky one falls apart.



**7. One simple verdict for humans, full detail for the AI**

People need one badge: overfit risk low, medium or high, with the reason in plain words. The AI needs every number in a format it can read, so it stops itself before you have to.



**8. Time is the only test that can't be gamed**

Once a strategy is published, every day after that is true out-of-sample. Show it that way, next to the range the backtest predicted, so you see early whether it's on track.



**What it costs to do this yourself**

People underestimate this part. Trading data alone (derivatives, sentiment, on-chain, options, macro) runs between $1,000 and $3,000 a month. Then someone has to work on it full-time: keeping every feed alive, re-checking timestamps, auditing that backtest and live still match. All in, you're looking at around $10,000 a month to run it properly. And it's never done.



**What I learned**

1. Stop asking the AI for the best strategy. Ask it to try to break the one you have.

2. Count your tries. Every variant is a lottery ticket.

3. Lock a final exam before you start, and open it once.

4. The backtest is the most optimistic number you'll ever see. Time since publish is the cheapest honest number.

5. Most "AI trading edges" are a timestamp bug or a missing cost.



Curious how others here handle this. If you let an agent run hundreds of backtests, how do you correct for it? Do you keep a holdout the agent can't touch?
